newsitem.title: RUSSIA: RUSSIA, NATO HOLD TENSE TALKS ON NEW RELATIONSHIP.
newsitem.headline: RUSSIA, NATO HOLD TENSE TALKS ON NEW RELATIONSHIP.

text.p: NATO and Russia are to hold highly sensitive talks on Tuesday on establishing a new modus vivendi in post-Cold War Europe.

Moscow, which stepped up its tough rhetoric on Monday in a now-familar negotiating tactic, will host NATO Secretary General Javier Solana for three hours of intense negotiations in the Russian capital.
Both sides are hoping for a breakthrough which will enable them to sign an accord laying out the terms for peaceful coexistence into the next century.
"Very much will depend (on Tuesday's talks)," Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov was quoted as saying by Itar-Tass news agency after visiting Paris last week.
The main sticking point is Russia's fear that the alliance's plans to invite in former Soviet bloc countries in July will lead to a military build-up near its borders.
Russia is also demanding a say in some decision-making under the accord, which it hopes to sign in six weeks.
Anxious to avoid potentially damaging point-scoring, the negotiators have agreed to keep the details of the talks under wraps, Russian officials said.
"The main thing is to reach a result, not to tell the world who did what to bring about the success," Interfax quoted a Russian foreign ministry source as saying.
But on the eve of the talks, both NATO and the Kremlin, under pressure from popular opinion, appeared prepared to dig in their heels rather than give any more ground.

Some NATO members "are not showing enough desire to seek a compromise," said Yeltsin's spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky, who this month took on extra responsibilities for coordinating foreign policy in the Kremlin.
"Such an agreement must be reached on an equal basis, but not at all costs," Yastrzhembsky told Interfax news agency.

In Brussels, diplomats said they were disappointed with the tough conditions laid down by Primakov in Paris, where they said he had effectively asked NATO to rule out any future military reinforcement of new alliance members.

NATO, which has sparked Russian charges it is creating new divisions in Europe with its enlargement plan, says it does not want the new members -- expected to be Poland, Hungary and the Czech republic -- to feel like a second class group.
Primakov also said in Paris that Russia hoped to sign a partnership document with NATO on May 27.

But the NATO diplomats said his negotiating stance looked like a step back from last month's Russian-U.S. summit in Helsinki, at which President Bill Clinton appeared to have more or less successfully defended the document on offer.
"It was depressingly hard line, a blast of cold air, going back on many of the things we thought we had sorted out -- particularly on military infrastructure," said a NATO military source.

"Solana is going to have to be very tough, we have made a generous offer which meets many Russian concerns. Whether Moscow takes it or not, enlargement is going ahead anyway," said a senior Western diplomat.
